title: The women who funded him (Luke 8:1–3)
hook: Mary Magdalene, Joanna, Susanna and many others ministered to him of their substance

segments.voice: Yesterday, a woman with an alabaster jar at Simon's dinner. Your line was go in peace. Did you love without counting? Day four hundred fifty-seven.

Here's a question the Gospels don't usually stop to answer: who paid for all this? Jesus and twelve men walking from town to town, for months, not fishing, not farming, not working for wages. Somebody bought the bread. Somebody paid for sandals and oil and a roof when there was one. Most of the time the Gospels skip the budget. Luke doesn't. In three short verses, tucked between bigger stories, he tells us exactly who kept the whole mission going. Today, the names.
screen: `WHO PAID FOR ALL THIS?` → `THIRTEEN MEN, NO WAGES.` → `THREE VERSES WITH THE ANSWER.`

segments.voice: Luke says Jesus went through the cities and towns preaching the kingdom, and the twelve were with him, and certain women. Then he names them. Mary, called Magdalene, out of whom seven devils had gone. Joanna, wife of Chusa, Herod's steward: a woman married to a man who managed the household of the king who would later mock Jesus. Susanna, about whom we know nothing else at all. And "many others who ministered unto him of their substance." Their substance means their own money and goods. These women weren't just along for the ride. They were paying for it. And ministered is a word worth stopping on. In Greek it's the verb diakoneo, to serve, the same root that gives the Church the word deacon. Luke uses it here for women who serve with what they own. Now follow these same women forward. Luke says the women who had followed him from Galilee stood at a distance and watched the crucifixion. They saw where he was laid. And on Sunday morning, Mary Magdalene and Joanna are named among the women who found the tomb empty and told the apostles. The ones who funded the road were the ones still there at the end. The Church remembers this. In 2016 Pope Francis raised the memorial of Mary Magdalene to a feast, and the decree honored her with an old title: apostle to the apostles. Many parishes still run on people like Joanna and Susanna, often women, often unnamed: the ones who count the collection, wash the linens, teach the children, and bring the casseroles. Luke wrote their names down.
screen: `MARY, JOANNA, SUSANNA, MANY OTHERS.` · `OF THEIR SUBSTANCE: THEIR OWN MONEY.` · `MINISTERED: THE DEACON WORD.` · `THE SAME WOMEN AT THE TOMB.` · then, large: `THEY MINISTERED OF THEIR SUBSTANCE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: thank the women who carry your parish, or your community. Settle, and breathe. Picture the place you belong: a parish, a school, a team, a family. Now look for the ones doing the work nobody announces. The woman who unlocks the door. The one who makes the coffee, keeps the list, remembers the birthdays. Pick one. Think of exactly what she gives. Decide how you'll thank her this week, by name, for something specific. If you pray, thank God for her. The bell holds the time.
Mary Magdalene. Named first among the women who funded Jesus' mission out of their own means, and stayed to the end, even at the tomb. Today's word.
Your line: they ministered of their substance. Today, thank one woman who carries something for your community, and say exactly what. Day four hundred fifty-seven.

howItsDone: The Church keeps the feast of Saint Mary Magdalene on July 22, and in many Catholic parishes women carry much of the daily work: catechesis, sacristy care, charity, music and administration.

fork.setup: you're Joanna, married to a steward in Herod's palace. a traveling preacher's group needs money to keep going. what do you do?
options: stay out of it; your husband's job is at stake.
give from your own means and go with them.
send a small gift and stay home.
fork.reveal: Luke names her among the women who traveled with him and ministered of their substance, and she's at the tomb on Easter morning.

original.note: Greek: they were serving, from diakoneo, the root of deacon.

trapdoor: what you thought: Jesus' followers were twelve men.
what it means: Luke says many women traveled with him too and paid for the mission from their own means.
what a scholar hears: diakoneo, the deacon verb, used for women's service; the same women are witnesses of the cross, burial and empty tomb.

sources.quoted: many others who ministered unto him of their substance

sources.ref: Congregation for Divine Worship, decree on the feast of Saint Mary Magdalene (2016)

notes: Confirm Douay-Rheims wording of Luke 8:3 ('who ministered unto him of their substance').
Some manuscripts read 'ministered unto them' rather than 'unto him'; confirm the Douay reading.
2016: Pope Francis raised the memorial of Mary Magdalene to a feast; the decree used the title 'apostle of the apostles' (apostolorum apostola). Confirm.
Herod Antipas mocking Jesus is Luke 23:11; confirm 'the king' is acceptable shorthand for the tetrarch.
Audit (10% sample): softened two unsourced sweeping claims ('every parish', 'most Catholic parishes') to 'many'.
